title: Diabetic emergency
summary: Give fast-acting glucose only when the person is alert and can swallow; call for altered consciousness or suspected ketoacidosis.
sources: 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid — Hypoglycemia
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026 — Hypoglycemia
actions: If the person is alert, can swallow safely, and has symptoms of low blood glucose, check glucose if possible and give about 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, preferably glucose tablets or gel as labelled.
Recheck symptoms and glucose after 15 minutes. If still low or symptomatic, repeat 15 g. After recovery, give a longer-acting snack if the next meal is not soon.
If swallowing is unsafe, a seizure occurs, or alertness is reduced, give nothing by mouth. Call emergency services and use the person’s prescribed glucagon if trained.
Deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, vomiting, or marked drowsiness may indicate severe high glucose or ketoacidosis and requires urgent medical care.
If the cause is uncertain or the person does not improve, call emergency services.
prohibitions: Do not give food or drink when swallowing is unsafe.
Do not give extra insulin or diabetes medicine unless it is part of the person’s own plan and they can manage it.

emergencyCall.text: Call emergency services for reduced consciousness, unsafe swallowing, seizure, new speech difficulty, deep laboured breathing, or failure to improve.
